case_study_insert.main_stem: Wren & Quill Booksellers (WQB) is a partnership in the independent book retail sector, employing a workforce of 34 across three bookshops in Elmsworth and an online store. Founded in 2016 by sisters Ada and Rosa Quill, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WQB plans to invest $425,000 in a second flagship shop with a reading cafe and click-and-collect hub, financed by a $270,000 bank loan and $155,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $187,500 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $15, and currently produces 42,000 units a year. WQB faces a growing operational problem: warehouse absenteeism has reached 8%, delaying online orders and raising overtime costs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Quarter 3 2026: The Elmsworth online hub dispatched 11,300 orders with a picking accuracy of 97.4%; 2.9% of parcels were reported damaged or incorrect. The reading cafe at the Quill Street shop recorded 1,850 transactions a week with food waste of 5.6%. Stock shrinkage was 1.6% of inventory value. A survey of 450 loyalty members found 63% discover new titles through social media, 38% would pay $8 a month for a reading club, and average online basket value is $34. Average delivery time is 1.9 days. Off-the-job training at the Elmsworth logistics college costs $720 per employee, while on-the-job training is led by senior pickers.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Wren & Quill Booksellers as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing interest costs for small retailers with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.15 to $12.90 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for hourly-paid retail and warehouse staff. (3) Paper and printing costs for publishers rose 9.8% year-on-year, inflation is running at 3.9%, and consumer spending on books and leisure grew 4.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WQB plans to finance its $425,000 second flagship shop with a $270,000 bank loan and $155,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for WQB of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs WQB nothing in interest or fees, which matters because the partnership already faces warehouse absenteeism of 8% and rising delivery pressure: the $155,000 portion of the $425,000 expansion funded internally carries no repayment duty at a time when cash is needed to keep the online hub dispatching 11,300 orders a quarter on a 1.9-day average delivery. Avoiding extra debt also insulates WQB from the central bank's latest base-rate rise to 5.25%, which would lift the cost of any variable-rate borrowing taken instead of retained profit.

Point 2: Keeping funding internal preserves the sisters' ownership and autonomy over the new shop, its reading cafe and its click-and-collect hub; no bank can impose trading covenants or demand security over personal assets. For a 34-person partnership in a sector where 4.1% growth in book spending is decent but not spectacular, lower fixed interest burdens protect the $15 selling price and the contribution each unit earns, leaving room to invest in member-focused offers such as the proposed $8-a-month reading club and to manage stock shrinkage of 1.6% without external pressure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wren & Quill Booksellers and its flagship expansion.

questions.question_text: WQB is launching its second flagship shop with a reading cafe. Consider a loyalty-member email campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WQB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Loyalty-member email campaign: Emailing WQB's 450 loyalty members is almost free, instantly measurable, and perfect for announcing the new shop, cafe opening hours and click-and-collect slots to customers who already buy an average basket of $34. Its ceiling is obvious, however: it reaches only existing members, so it cannot pull in new shoppers for a launch event designed to broaden local awareness in Elmsworth, and repeated emails risk unsubscribes if overused.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is relatively cheap, reaches a broad Elmsworth audience at breakfast and drive time, and can carry repeated memorable messages about the cafe and in-store events, suiting the launch's family audience. Its drawbacks are limited targeting, no direct clickable call to action, and fading reach among younger readers who increasingly discover books through social media, which 63% of WQB's own survey respondents said they use.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with local bookstagram and booktok creators matches the 63% of members who discover new titles through social media, showcases the cafe visually, and creates shareable launch content. Engagement is measurable and the cost per young customer reached is low, though results depend on choosing authentic creators and sustaining posts beyond launch week.

Recommendation: WQB should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact discovery channel its research identifies, combines reach with measurability, and is affordable for a partnership funding a $425,000 expansion. Local radio is rejected as too broad and untargeted for a shop-plus-cafe opening that needs measurable footfall; the email campaign, while cheap and useful for existing members, is rejected as the lead channel because it cannot grow awareness beyond the 450-member base; WQB should still email members first as a low-cost warmup to the influencer launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to WQB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WQB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WQB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio sponsorship and the email-only approach are rejected.

questions.question_text: WQB's warehouse absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for WQB of using democratic leadership to reduce it.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership involves the 34 employees in scheduling, workload and picking workflows rather than imposing them, which raises ownership and job satisfaction among warehouse staff. Workers who help design shift patterns and rest breaks face less fatigue and are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking the 8% absenteeism rate that delays online orders and forces costly overtime at the Elmsworth hub.

Point 2: Consulting pickers and managers surfaces practical fixes a top-down approach misses, for example reorganising the fastest-moving fiction sections near packing stations to cut walking time, or buddying new staff with senior pickers to lift the already-strong 97.4% picking accuracy. Lower absenteeism protects the 1.9-day delivery promise that underpins WQB's $34 average online basket, and it reduces disruption to the cafe and shop teams. Because WQB already operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, extending it costs nothing and supports retention of the 34-strong team while the partnership asks more of everyone ahead of the second flagship opening and its $8-a-month reading club launch.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WQB's absenteeism, picking accuracy and delivery promise.

questions.question_text: WQB needs to lift picking accuracy above 97.4% and reduce damaged or incorrect parcels. Consider on-the-job training in the online hub or off-the-job training at the Elmsworth logistics college. Which should WQB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training in the online hub is exactly matched to WQB's layout, barcode systems and packing materials; senior pickers can demonstrate packing, checking and escalation routines in context, protecting the 97.4% picking accuracy and attacking the 2.9% damaged-or-incorrect rate. It costs nothing in fees, keeps staff productive and lets corrections happen instantly against real orders flowing at 11,300 per quarter. Weaknesses are that senior pickers lose productive picking time, inconsistencies between trainers can spread errors, and there is no formal certificate to show external auditors or insurers.

Off-the-job training: The Elmsworth logistics college at $720 per employee provides structured inventory, health-and-safety and dispatch modules with a certificate, and removes staff from daily pressure while they learn. If the whole 34-person workforce attended, the fees alone would total $24,480 (34 x $720), plus cover costs for their absence, and because WQB is opening a second flagship, that disruption lands exactly when capacity is stretched and the 11,300-order dispatch schedule cannot slip. The content is generic and would still need tailoring to the hub's layout afterwards.

Decision: WQB should choose on-the-job training as the primary fix, sending one or two team leads to college for a certificate in logistics benchmarking. On-the-job training is free in fees, immediate, and specific to the hub, and avoids $24,480 of fees plus absence cover during the flagship launch and the cafe conversion. Full off-the-job training for all staff is rejected as unaffordable and disruptive; a small college investment for leads captures the external standard without removing the picking team or risking the 11,300-order dispatch promise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WQB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of WQB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of WQB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the online hub.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WQB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $187,500 / ($15 - $9) = $187,500 / $6 = 31,250 units. Answer: break-even output is 31,250 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15 - $9 = $6. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WQB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. WQB can compare the 31,250-unit break-even output with actual output of 42,000 units to confirm the bookshops and online store clear fixed costs with a margin of safety of 10,750 units, giving confidence to open the second flagship before committing further capital.
2. The $6 contribution per unit lets managers test launch-week pricing; a 15% launch discount would cut the selling price to $12.75 and contribution to $3.75, so managers can see immediately that deep discounting would need heavy extra volume to protect the $187,500 fixed costs.
3. Knowing break-even output helps set performance thresholds for the new flagship and cafe; managers can require the shop to add enough units to hold more than 10,750 units of headroom before agreeing any extra hire or refit cost.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($187,500 / 42,000 units + $9 = $13.46 per book) to spot rising waste, given shrinkage at 1.6% of inventory value and cafe food waste of 5.6%, and decide whether to renegotiate the $9 variable cost with distributors as paper and printing costs rise 9.8%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 31,250 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs the 42,000-unit output; launch discount modelling against the $6 contribution and $187,500 fixed costs; flagship and cafe threshold setting; and unit-cost tracking at $13.46 to attack shrinkage and food waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WQB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WQB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.53 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.68 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $85,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $52,000 + $135,000 = $352,000. Ratio 2024 = $275,000 / $180,000 = 1.53; 2025 = $352,000 / $210,000 = 1.68. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($275,000 - $150,000) / $180,000 = $125,000 / $180,000 = 0.69; 2025 = ($352,000 - $165,000) / $210,000 = $187,000 / $210,000 = 0.89.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The coverage of current assets over current liabilities improved from 1.53 to 1.68, and the quick measure excluding inventories improved from 0.69 to 0.89, helped by cash and equivalents rising from $85,000 to $135,000 while current liabilities grew from $180,000 to $210,000. Trade receivables rose only from $40,000 to $52,000, which is safe for an online-and-shops retailer whose sales are mostly paid by card at the till or online before dispatch. Inventories edged up from $150,000 to $165,000 ahead of the $425,000 flagship opening and the click-and-collect hub, so the stock build should unwind as footfall arrives.

Conclusion: WQB's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.53 to 1.68) and the acid test ratio (0.69 to 0.89) show stronger short-term solvency, and cash, rather than inventories, is driving the improvement. WQB should still watch the 2.9% damaged-or-incorrect rate and cafe food waste of 5.6% to keep cash conversion strong, but the trend comfortably supports the $425,000 second flagship.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether WQB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WQB of installing a click-and-collect hub in the new flagship shop.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Click-and-collect converts the 450 loyalty members and online browsers who already buy an average basket of $34 into footfall for the new flagship, where the 63% who discover titles through social media can then browse the reading cafe, attend events and pick up reserved orders without paying delivery. It cuts last-mile delivery cost versus home drop-off, turns collections into impulse purchases, and strengthens WQB's local positioning against pure-play online rivals, supporting the whole $425,000 expansion case and the 1.9-day delivery promise that keeps members loyal to an independent shop.

Disadvantage: The hub adds shelving, staffing and handling costs on top of the cafe's 5.6% food waste problem and 1.6% stock shrinkage, and if parcels are not ready on time it damages the very 1.9-day promise that differentiates WQB online; that failure mode already sits behind the 2.9% damaged-or-incorrect rate. Poor stock control would also tie up cash in unsold, slow-moving titles on top of the $165,000 inventory balance, so WQB must pair click-and-collect with tight picking routines and clear collection logging before launch, or the new revenue channel could erode the $6 contribution per unit it is meant to protect.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WQB's members, delivery promise and waste problems.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in paper and printing costs will affect WQB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If WQB's $270,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the additional annual cost is 0.75% x $270,000 = $2,025 a year (0.0075 x $270,000). That is modest against $187,500 of fixed costs and could be avoided entirely by fixing the rate; the bigger effect is psychological, raising the hurdle for any further borrowing beyond the flagship and squeezing consumer confidence on discretionary purchases such as hardback novels and the $8 reading club.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.90 per hour): WQB's warehouse, cafe and shop teams include hourly-paid workers, so the rise flows straight into payroll and is unavoidable. No hours or pay rates are stated in the insert, so a firm total cannot be invented; judged against productivity, 42,000 units / 34 employees = 1,235.3 units per employee, the wage cost per unit stays manageable only if the 97.4% picking accuracy holds and absenteeism falls below 8%. Any slip raises unit labour cost and squeezes the $6 contribution per unit.

Paper and printing cost rise (9.8% year-on-year): Publisher input inflation is the change that scales across everything WQB sells. As an explicit upper bound built from insert figures, if the whole $9 variable cost reflected publisher paper inflation it would add 9.8% x $9 = $0.88 per unit; at 42,000 units a year that is about $37,000 a year (42,000 x $0.88 = $36,960), cutting contribution from $6 toward $5.12. Cover prices rarely move by 9.8%, so margins will likely absorb part of it; 3.9% inflation and 4.1% growth in book and leisure spending help demand, but WQB cannot fully recover the gap without pricing itself off competitors.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in paper and printing costs will have the greatest impact. It applies across every one of the 42,000 units sold, unlike the fixed $2,025 annual interest effect or the bounded wage rise, which depends on hours not stated; and unlike the wage rise, it directly attacks the $6 contribution that funds the flagship and reading cafe. WQB should widen its mix toward higher-margin sidelines such as the $8 reading club and gift lines to offset it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WQB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WQB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WQB with a well-justified judgement that paper and printing cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
